newsitem.title: USA: S. Korean jumbo jet crashes in Guam with 254 aboard.
newsitem.headline: S. Korean jumbo jet crashes in Guam with 254 aboard.

text.p: A Korean Air Lines jetliner with 254 people on board crashed and burned on Guam early on Wednesday, but officials said as many as 30 passengers may have survived.
An airline official said Korean Air Lines Flight 801, a Boeing 747-300, was en route from Seoul when it crashed in a hilly jungle area just miles from the airport.
Eduardo Cruz, a doctor at Guam Memorial Hospital, said staff members could see the flaming wreckage from the hospital miles away.
"We didn't hear anything, but we walked out and looked up and there was a big fireball on the mountain," Cruz told KCAL TV in Los Angeles.
The hospital was about six miles (10 km) from the crash site.
Cruz said the site of the crash was "very dense, rugged terrain" and that it had been raining "rather heavily" in the last 2-3 days.
Korean Air Lines said 254 people were aboard. Airline spokesman Suh Kang-Yoon told Reuters in Seoul the plane was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crew.
Earlier another KAL official put the total at 257 -- 234 passengers and 23 crewmembers.
As many as 30 people were believed to have survived.
"We believe there are 29 to 30 survivors and most have been taken to the Navy medical centre," Andrew Murphy, spokesman for the Guam Airport Authority, told Reuters by telephone.
Jim Hall, chairman of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, told a news conference in Seattle that as many as 13 U.S. citizens were believed to have been on the flight.
A massive rescue effort, using U.S. Sea Knight helicopters and bulldozers to cut through the jungle, was immediately launched and all area hospitals were put on alert.

"We are in an emergency mode preparing to accept casualties. We are getting out every ounce of plasma we have and my understanding is the U.S. Navy Hospital is doing the same," Harry Fornas, a spokesman for Guam Memorial Hospital, told Reuters by telephone.
U.S. Navy helicopters were flying survivors to area hospitals.
The Federal Aviation Administration launched an investigation into the cause but early reports said weather or engine troubles may have been a factor.
An FAA spokeswoman said the plane had just been cleared for landing at 2:35 a.m. local time on Wednesday (12:35 p.m. EDT on Tuesday) (1635 GMT on Tuesday) when radar contact was lost.
Air safety sources said visibility at the time was limited to about one mile (1.6 km) due to the heavy rain.
An emergency field hospital was set up by U.S. Navy personnel as close to the wreckage as possible.
A spokeswoman for the Guam governor's office said the wreckage was scattered, and there were reports of several explosions heard after the impact, with blue and orange flames.
Spokeswoman Ginger Cruz said some survivors had broken limbs, some were lying down, and most serious ones were immediately taken to hospitals by helicopter.

Boeing Co. flight safety engineers were preparing to fly to Guam to assist U.S. officials investigating the crash. The engineers were waiting for official confirmation of the crash, Boeing spokesman Doug Webb said.
Webb said the jet involved was a Boeing 747-300 delivered to Korean Air in December 1984. The jet had accumulated just under 50,000 hours of flight time in 8,433 flights or "cycles," he said.
While the cause of the crash was unknown, there were unconfirmed reports the plane was experiencing engine problems. In addiiton, some flights were delayed due to heavy rains.

Guam, largest of the Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific, is an unincorporated territory of the United States with a population of about 144,000. A U.S. military base covers about one-third of the island, the westernmost U.S. territory.
